these segments carried an evangelist framing clause, so there was nothing to
split and nothing to move out of red.

n5 was retelling these two verses in modern English while the verses themselves
were missing, which left jv11's 'if ye then, being evil' resting on a picture the
viewer had only heard described. Now the real verse speaks first.

EDIT TO EXISTING NARRATOR TEXT: n5 is split at its own seam. n5 keeps only its
lead-in sentence - 'Then Jesus makes it personal with a picture from any home.'
- and hands to jv910. Its remaining four sentences become n5b, unchanged word for
word, now functioning as the retelling. All three beats stay on S7, so the
picture is unchanged.

WOMEN: Matthew 7 records no woman speaking. Nothing was added rather than
reaching outside the chapter for one.

WHY-LAW: prayer is not technique and not endurance. It is a child putting out its
hands to a Father who is glad to be asked. Milk framing - just ask.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: People have always wondered how prayer really works. Do you have to say it just right? Wear God down? Jesus, teaching on a hillside, made it startlingly simple.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three words, and each one is warmer and more personal than the last. Ask — like a child who simply puts out its hands, trusting, expecting good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seek — more than a word now; it is getting up and searching, patient and hopeful, sure that what you are looking for is really there to be found.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Knock — and keep knocking — on a door you cannot yet see behind. And the promise is that the door does open. Not maybe. Not for the specially worthy. Every one who asks, receives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus makes it personal with a picture from any home.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone? Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A child asks its father for bread. What kind of father hands his hungry child a stone instead? Or a snake when he asks for a fish? No father you would trust.

segments.speaker: jesus
segments.text: If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: How much more. If flawed, tired, imperfect parents still love to give their kids good things — how much more does a perfect Father delight to give to you? Prayer is not twisting God's arm. It is a child asking a good Father who is glad to be asked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the invitation is just this: ask. Not perfectly. Not impressively. Simply, honestly, like a child. The Father is not reluctant. He is leaning in, glad to hear your voice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Ask, seek, knock. Jesus says your Father in heaven is far kinder than the best parent you can imagine, and glad to be asked. Is there something you have been afraid to ask him for?

stills_wanted.S7: S7 now carries three beats - the lead-in, Matthew 7:9-10 verbatim, and the retelling - so it has to hold the whole bread-and-stone picture on its own. Frame the moment of asking, not of giving: a small child at a plain table with both hands open and lifted toward a father who is already reaching for the loaf. Warm indoor light, an ordinary kitchen, no stone and no serpent anywhere in frame. The absurdity lives in the words; the image should show only the kindness the words argue from.
